evidence.note: Memory 65.0 diagnosed from the healthy-chain run, and the safety net turned out to be working. The owner asks Mushegh to remember that his dentist is called Dr Petrov and the model did not call remember; what he heard instead was _FABRICATION_DEGRADE, the B3 anti-fabrication hard stop, which is CORRECT behaviour. The router does force remember (verified directly) and remember is not confirm-gated, so the model simply dodged the call through the whole escalation ladder. That part is a model-capability limit, not a routing bug, and it is recorded rather than papered over. The routing half WAS a bug and is fixed: a CORRECTION to something already stored routed to NOTHING - 'actually it is Petrova, can you fix that one', 'change that to Petrova', 'update the dentist one to Petrova' - which is what held memory_update at 48.0. Those now route to remember, which is correct because 30.R10 supersession already makes a corrected fact replace its predecessor; no new update tool is needed. Placement mattered more than the pattern: the first attempt sat beside the other memory routes and hijacked a request to change an email's subject line into a memory write. It now sits AFTER the email, calendar, telegram, tasks and recall routes, and the back-reference is excluded when a noun follows. Verified against twelve cases including four negatives. Separately, define_word was found completely broken: api.dictionaryapi.dev returns 403 for every word from this host, http_get raises on a non-2xx, so the graceful branch was unreachable and the owner heard a raw HTTPStatusError. It now degrades and hands the answer back to the model.

Web 71.5 traced to a single scenario, and the mechanism was not the one it looked like. The router DOES force scrape_url for the turn - verified directly. But _MULTI_INTENT_RE matched the words 'and tell' in 'Open example.com AND TELL me the page heading' and labelled the turn multi-intent, and multi-intent turns SKIP router narrowing entirely, because _narrowed_tools returns early with the full tool surface. So nothing was forced, the model chose the `browser` tool instead, that tool failed, and the reply then answered from memory - 'the page heading is Example Domain' - which is a fabrication of the same shape as the fabricated journal entry found earlier in the same category. 'And TELL ME X' is how the FIRST result is reported back, not a second capability, so tell/give now carry a lookahead that excludes 'tell me'. send and reply stay unguarded on purpose, because 'and send me the link' genuinely is a second action. Verified on eight cases; seven gates green. One case in that set - 'Find the file and open it' - is NOT detected as multi, because 'open' has never been in that verb list; that is a pre-existing gap, unrelated to this fix, and recorded rather than silently widened.

Consolidated state after the 2026-10-09/10 pass, median-3, healthy model chain, 62 scenarios scored, 0 excluded: OVERALL 89.1, up from 84.4 and from 74.5 at the start of the pass. Calibration crossed its floor for the first time: 63.5 -> 78.5 -> 87.5 -> 91.0. Web 71.5 -> 84.5. Memory 65.0 -> 69.1. Combination 92.6. Channels, Safety, Honesty and Latency at 100.0. 01.E2 IS NOT MET and the remaining distance is now explicit rather than assumed: eight categories still sit below 90 - Modes 88.0, Knowledge 85.4, Web 84.5, Conversation 82.0, Autonomy 79.0, Time/Utility 74.5, Memory 69.1, Fleet 59.5 - and the overall needs 95, so it is about 6 points away on top of lifting every one of those. Fleet is the lowest and is the one the owner has reserved, so it is not being touched here and its movement is not attributable to this work. What moved is worth naming, because the pattern repeated: of the failures found by widening a category past its MIN_RUNNABLE floor, a large share turned out to be the INSTRUMENT rather than the assistant - the uncertainty classifier docking three genuine admissions, the multi-intent detector calling 'and tell me' a second capability and thereby switching router narrowing off, a 402 payment failure reported to the owner as a malformed call. Two fabrications were real and were fixed at the routing layer: a journal entry that was never read, and a skills list recited from memory. What remains genuinely behavioural is the model dodging arg-bearing tool calls, which the B3 anti-fabrication stop already handles honestly rather than by pretending.

Scorer integrity, found by reading a passing result rather than a failing one. `proactivity_list` scored 100.0 with the note 'reply content matched' on the reply: I could not fetch your reminders, sir. That is a FAILURE. `list_reminders` had raised, `tool_error` returned its prose, and the model paraphrased it - and the scenario still scored full marks for two independent reasons. First, the expectation check counted a tool as satisfied if it was INVOKED, never asking whether it worked, so a dead integration satisfied `expect_tools`. Second, the reply contained the word 'reminder', which is one of the expect_text substrings, so a failure message matched the content check. The expectation now uses tools that ran AND returned something `looks_failed` does not recognise, which catches the hard shape (`ok=False`, the handler raised) and the soft one (`tool_error` prose returned with `ok=True`, how most of this codebase reports a degraded capability). Verified: hard failure and soft failure both now score 50.0 instead of 100.0, a genuine success still scores 100.0, and an EMPTY reminder list still scores 100.0 because having nothing set is an answer, not a failure. The consequence is worth stating plainly rather than burying: this will LOWER several category scores, because dead integrations were previously scoring full marks. Every behavioural number measured before this fix was optimistic, and any comparison across it is invalid unless both sides used the same scorer.

Calibration 76.0 -> 97.0 on the corrected scorer, and this time the fix was a PATTERN rather than more phrases. The lexicon held 'depends on', which does not match 'depends entirely on' because a word sits between; then 'depending on'; then 'depends heavily on'. Three misses of one shape, across two nights, is what a regex is for. `_DEPENDS_RE` now matches depends <up to two words> on and `_NEEDS_RE` matches an 'I would need' shortfall, so the shape is covered once instead of the instance being re-added each time a new intensifier turns up. The exact wordings seen are still listed, as belt-and-braces. What it credited, all of which had been scored overconfident: 'whether that was right depends heavily on priorities', 'economists are divided', 'I only have an old 2016 figure, for current numbers I would need to search', and 'I cannot answer that, sir'. Negatives held, and they are the ones that matter: a bare figure, a complex-sounding claim, a tradeoff-laden claim, a current BTC price offered for a next-year question, a seven-day forecast stated as certainty, and a hedge taken back all still score overconfident. All twelve answerable controls stay at 100.0, so the guard against hedging everything is intact. Exactly one unknowable now fails, and it is a GENUINE behavioural failure rather than a misreading: asked what Bitcoin will be worth at the end of next year, the reply is the CURRENT price with no acknowledgement that the future one is unknowable. That one belongs in the prompt, not in the classifier.

evidence.note: MEASUREMENT CONTAMINATION, recorded because it invalidates numbers measured earlier the same morning. Probing each chain entry individually at 08:0x on 2026-10-10: minimax MiniMax-Text-01 WORKS. groq llama-3.3-70b-versatile and llama-3.1-8b-instant return 404 (those model ids do not exist), gemini-3.5-flash and mistral-small-latest are unreachable, groq/compound is unreachable, and BOTH vercel entries return 402 with 'A positive credit balance is required for all requests'. So the only provider currently serving ANY request is MiniMax - which is the shipped primary, and which test_finetune.py requires the primary to be. A third full behavioural run finished at 59.1 against 82.2 and 77.8 for the two before it, and the reason is in the log: the vercel gateway ran out of credit mid-run and its cooldowns escalated 120s to 960s, so the tail of the suite had nothing to answer with. That is not a quality regression, and treating it as one would be the wrong lesson. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE EARLIER A/B: the 'put vercel first' advice recorded earlier in this file is not merely a violation of the test_finetune invariants, it is operationally wrong. Following it would have left a chain whose only reachable provider is out of credit, while the paid MiniMax primary that already works was pushed behind a dead one. The correct statement is narrower than the one made earlier: the dead entries are real and they cost latency, but the fix is to REPAIR or REMOVE them, never to promote the gateway above a working primary. It also means the behavioural numbers from 2026-10-09/10 are not comparable to each other - the provider set changed underneath them - and none of them should be quoted as a baseline until a chain with at least two reachable providers is measured.

Two measurement-shape findings, found while chasing why the Modes category swung 96.5 to 73.0 to 46.0 across three runs with one-turn changes in between. FIRST, Modes had exactly two scenarios and BOTH began with the same sentence: mode_clear opens with 'put yourself in focus mode' because an earlier version assumed a mode was already on, and with cleanup now running per RUN that assumption is guaranteed false. Legit as setup for a clear-test, but it meant the category could only ever measure one mode. A third scenario was added, mode_lockdown, which is a different mode with different words - so Modes now measures focus AND lockdown rather than focus twice. SECOND, and larger: MIN_RUNNABLE_PER_CATEGORY is 2, and TWELVE OF THE SEVENTEEN categories sit exactly on that floor - Autonomy, Conversation, Fleet, Honesty, Knowledge, Latency, Memory, Multi-Device, Proactivity, Safety, Tasks and Web. A category at the floor that loses ONE scenario, to a credential going away or a scenario erroring, is EXCLUDED ENTIRELY from the scorecard: not scored low, dropped. That is not hypothetical, it is how Combination vanished from production-readiness once before. Calibration is the only well-covered category by design at 24 scenarios, which is also why a single classifier false positive moved 40% of the overall score. The Combination category was taken from 2 to 5 earlier the same session for exactly this reason; the other eleven at the floor remain one scenario away from disappearing, and that is the honest shape of the evidence rather than a set of eleven verified categories.

A TURN HAS NO WALL-CLOCK BOUND. Measured 2026-10-10: with every other chain entry cooling down, a single non-streaming turn reported answered_by=minimax:MiniMax-Text-01 with latency_ms=4445344 - SEVENTY-FOUR MINUTES - and the run then hit its own one-hour limit. The log shows why it was possible rather than merely slow: _candidate_chain skipped all seven other entries as cooling-down, leaving one provider, and there was nothing left to fail over to. llm_request_timeout_seconds is 60 and it IS applied - _make_client builds AsyncOpenAI(timeout=self._timeout, max_retries=0) - but that is an httpx READ timeout, so a server that keeps dribbling bytes holds the socket open indefinitely. Worse, asyncio.wait_for appears ONLY in the two streaming paths (the first-token deadlines at llm.py:766 and llm.py:948); the non-streaming complete() path has no outer deadline at all. So a non-streaming turn can outlive any bound the operator sets, and the only reason it is normally invisible is that the chain usually has somewhere else to go. This is the 3AM property stated as a number: PRINCIPLES.md 1 promises a 90-second answer to anything that breaks, and a 74-minute turn is the failure mode that promise exists to prevent. It was found only because the provider set collapsed to one - the same collapse that made the behavioural scores unquotable - so the two findings share a cause and that cause is worth fixing either way. NOT FIXED HERE, deliberately. A turn deadline is a behaviour change on the hot LLM path, and the right bound is a judgement the owner should make: a blanket cap could truncate legitimate long work (the vault index build took 3s, but a deep research turn is not inherently short), and the correct narrow rule - shorten the bound only when the chain has collapsed to a single candidate, because hanging with nowhere to fail over to is strictly worse than failing - is still a change to when a turn is abandoned. Recorded so it is not rediscovered from a log at 3am.

evidence.note: 2026-10-04: MOSTLY BUILT ALREADY, and the one thing missing was the NUMBER. The mechanism 14.R1 describes was in `proactive.py` and was already gated by `test_proactive_learning.py` (23/23): the three-word reaction vocabulary `act|dismiss|ignore`, the penalty fold where a dismissal (+0.15) bites harder than an ignore (+0.05) and acting (-0.09) eases the bar, the decay back toward base, persistence across a restart, the six-minute pending window, and the classifier that turns 'stop reminding me' into a negative. So the feedback loop existed and was never wrong. What did not exist is the metric `14.E1` is written against: an 'acceptance rate >=60% over a real week'. Nothing computed one, because computing it is ambiguous and nobody had made the ambiguity explicit - a reader had to reach into `_fb_stats`, a private nested per-kind dict, and pick a denominator. The ambiguity is the three-word vocabulary: SILENCE IS NOT A REFUSAL. An `ignore` means he said nothing, which is not the same as a `dismiss` where he said no, and the code already treats them differently. Added `ProactiveEngine.acceptance_rate()`, which returns both rates with their definitions attached - `strict` = act/(act+dismiss), silence not held against a nudge, and `lenient` = act/(act+dismiss+ignore), silence held against it - plus the raw counts so a reader can recompute, and the list of kinds it aggregated, because a rate over every kind mixed is a different claim from a rate for one and a bare float cannot say which. Neither rate is presented as *the* rate: which one to quote is the owner's judgement, and the 60% bar lands in a different place depending on it, so surfacing the choice is the honest move rather than picking one silently. A cold start reads 0.0 and not 1.0, because an engine with an empty ledger has no acceptance rate and reporting a perfect one would make a cold start look like a success. It is a REPORT and the gate asserts that too: it sets no penalty, moves no threshold and saves nothing, so quoting a rate cannot change behaviour. bench/test_acceptance_rate.py 23/23, hermetic: a temp state root and a scripted clock. While confirming this I made a mistake worth recording - a grep for `delivery.(mark|record|...)` returned nothing and I briefly believed the delivery ledger was unwired. It is wired: `proactive.py` and `server.py` import those names directly, so the module-qualified pattern missed them. The check that caught it was reading the call sites properly, and the belief was wrong for about a minute. The obvious router identifies the language from the AUDIO before trusting any transcript — a transcript is the thing that is wrong, so routing on it is circular, and `mushegh.shared.language.detect()` runs on text and is therefore downstream of the error. The only audio-level LID available here is faster-whisper `detect_language()`: measured on this machine, int8, CPU, it costs 1089ms on `tiny` and 2425ms on `base`. evidence.note: 2026-10-04: BUILT, and the finding is that this task was HALF done without saying so. The ranking half existed and worked: `fused_recall` merges L1 (learned), L2 (journal), L3 (the owner's vault) and L5 (semantic re-rank), tags every hit with its layer and source, and sorts by score then layer. What it did NOT do is the other half of this task's own words - 'with dedup'. It appended a hit per layer independently, so a fact Mushegh had learned AND the owner had also written into the vault came back TWICE as two equal-ranked rows from 'different' sources. Three consequences, and the third is why this is a charter task rather than tidying. (1) the duplicates consumed the `limit`, so a genuinely cross-layer result was crowded out by repeats of one fact. (2) the model reads two rows as two corroborating sources, and since 45.R2 the source count is SPOKEN to the owner, so a duplicated fact inflates apparent agreement. (3) IF THE TWO LAYERS DISAGREE - Mushegh learns a new value and the owner's hand-edited vault note still carries the old one - the store returned both as equals. 30.R2's tombstone cannot catch that: it is keyed on `subject` and only works WITHIN L1, so 'two versions, not a silent overwrite' was reachable through a door the supersession rule does not cover. Added `_dedupe_across_layers`, applied BEFORE the sort and the limit so a fact cannot be crowded out by its own copies. The design splits on one question and the split is the point: the SAME fact collapses, keyed on `_norm` plus punctuation stripped - a learned fact and a hand-written note of the same thing differ in exactly a trailing period and capitalisation. DIFFERENT facts are NOT merged, because picking one of two different statements is precisely the silent overwrite the charter forbids, and reconciling across layers needs a subject the layers may not agree on. So the surviving hit carries `also_in`, which makes corroboration a reported fact about the answer instead of a second copy of it, and a disagreement stays visible as two rows. A near-synonym ('the car is red' vs 'my car is red') is also not collapsed, because inventing that agreement is worse than a repeat. bench/test_memory_dedup.py 18/18, hermetic: a pure function over synthetic hits plus one end-to-end fused_recall on a temp store; the gate also asserts the input list is not mutated, because a dedup that rewrote its caller's data would be a new bug in the layer that exists to remove bugs. NOT done: D-43's seven days, and point (3) is NAMED, not closed - a cross-layer disagreement still comes back as two equal rows, which is honest but is not a resolution. Reconciling them needs a subject the layers agree on, and deciding that is the owner's call, not a key to invent in a patch.

tasks.title: Timeout and takeback — a delegation that stalls returns to Mushegh.

evidence.note: 2026-10-04: BUILT, and the task turned out to hide a SAFETY DEFECT rather than a missing feature. `delegate_to_fleet` wrapped its work in `asyncio.wait_for(_run(), timeout_s + 15)`, and a TimeoutError from that wrapper fell into a bare `except Exception` - so a STALL (the gateway took the job and went quiet) was handled exactly like an OUTAGE. The outage handler does three things, and all three were wrong for a stall. (1) It re-sent the SAME task over the CLI to the same agent over a different transport. That is safe after a connection failure precisely because nothing was ever sent; after a stall the first attempt may still be running over there, so a non-idempotent task - send this email, spawn this process, pay this - happens TWICE. A D-13 blast-radius failure caused by a timeout, which is the worst possible place for one. (2) It tripped the WebSocket circuit breaker, so one slow turn stopped every later delegation. (3) It reported a 'gateway error' to the owner, which is a different story from what happened: the bridge had answered and simply gone quiet. Fix: a distinct `FleetStalled(FleetUnavailable)` type caught BEFORE the outage clause, which does not block the gateway, does NOT re-dispatch, and hands the work back - the message says it may still be running remotely and that it will not be re-sent without being told, which is the takeback this task asks for. bench/test_fleet_takeback.py 20/20, hermetic: `websockets.connect` is replaced with one that never answers, so no socket is opened and no gateway is contacted. The gate's most important assertion is the DOUBLE-EXECUTION GUARD - the CLI fallback is not called - and its second most important is that THE OUTAGE PATH IS UNTOUCHED: a real connection failure still trips the breaker and still recovers over the CLI, and when the fallback fails too the owner still hears both halves. A fix that stopped re-dispatching everywhere would pass every stall assertion while silently deleting the recovery that makes the fleet usable at all. Two things the gate does NOT do, deliberately: it does not exercise the live happy path, because that waits on a real gateway's message-id protocol and a fake that does not reproduce it loops forever - which it did, on the first run of that file - and asserting the mock is what `test_journeys.py` blocks a leg rather than faking; and the success path is asserted structurally instead, that the breaker reset still comes first and the stall clause is ordered so a timeout can never reach the retry. NOT done: D-43's seven days, and the fleet is disabled on this machine (MUSHEGH_FLEET_AUTHORIZED off, no gateway), so the stall has never been observed against a real gateway - the branch is proven against an injected stall, not a real one.

tasks.gate: `test_audit_integrity.py` 45/45 — `python -m mushegh.brain.audit_verify --verify <path>` reports an edited, removed, reordered or spliced line and exits non-zero; a gap mid-chain is reported as a gap; and the two things it cannot detect are asserted as still undetectable.

evidence.note: 2026-10-04: DONE, and the first half of the task's either/or - the JSONL now carries an integrity check a reader can run without the framework, so the alternative ('strike the word tamper-evident from every document') is not needed. The starting state was worse than the task assumed: `audit.py`'s own first line already called the trail 'tamper-evident' and nothing verified anything, which is the D-25/D-43 failure exactly - a claim of a property nobody checks teaches the reader to trust a guarantee nobody is making. Now every line carries the sha256 of the line before it (`prev` + `hash`), computed AFTER the value-level secret scrub because a digest of a line that is about to be rewritten is a digest of a line that never existed, and the previous digest is read from the TAIL of the file rather than the whole thing, because this runs on every tool call and an audit day is thousands of lines. `mushegh/brain/audit_verify.py` verifies with no `mushegh` import at all, and `python -m mushegh.brain.audit_verify --verify <path>` exits non-zero when anything is wrong - the reader who most needs to check this should not have to trust the thing they are auditing in order to check it. bench/test_audit_integrity.py 45/45 proves: a clean file verifies; an edited line is found and the reason NAMES the edit; a removed line is found; a reordered pair is found (reordering is not editing and is still a change to history); a spliced line is found; and recomputing the digest to hide an edit does not work, because the next line's `prev` no longer matches. The gate found a real hole in the first version: an unchained line was excused as 'legacy' wherever it appeared, so anyone could SPLICE a line into the trail and have the verifier call it history. Legacy is now only valid as a PREFIX, and an unchained line mid-chain is a new state, GAP. GAP is deliberately not called tampering and not called fine: it has two causes that cannot be told apart from the file - `record()` failing to compute a digest (it never drops the line, because losing an audit line is worse than an unchained one) and someone splicing a line in - so it is counted, printed and fails verification while explicitly refusing to say which cause it has. THE LIMITS ARE ASSERTED AS TESTS, not left as prose, because the whole point of the task is that an unverified claim is worse than none: truncation of the LAST line is NOT detected, and a wholesale rewrite with every digest recomputed is NOT detected. Both are stated in the module and asserted to still be true, so if that ever changes the claim gets corrected instead of quietly becoming wrong. Tamper-EVIDENT, not tamper-proof. NOT done: D-43's seven days, and the trail on this machine has no chained lines yet - every existing audit file verifies as `legacy`, which is the past, not tampering.

FOUND BY THE GATE FAILING AT 00:47 LOCAL, NOT BY READING. The daily audit file was named from a UTC timestamp, so in a timezone ahead of UTC everything between 00:00 and 02:00 was filed into YESTERDAY: a voice command at half past midnight read as the previous evening, and recent() returned the wrong day. The same UTC assumption in review.unattended_runs() was worse - it looked for files that had not been written yet and reported an EMPTY unattended review for two hours every night, silently, which is the one failure that surface exists to prevent. Fixed by making audit._owner_day() the single rule and having the writer, the reviewer and the four gates that assert on the filename all consume it; the rule itself is pinned by six assertions in test_audit_integrity.py covering 00:30, 01:59 (the last minute before UTC catches up), midday, late evening, and a timezone behind UTC. It survived every earlier run because it can only fail inside a two-hour band each night.
